Image from Pixabay

Trade Desk (TTD) shares fell 76.3% in the year to October 13, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned about 18%. The advertising technology company reported slower revenue growth in each of the past four quarters. In the August 6, 2026 report, growth had fallen short of management's own expectations. How far did Trade Desk's growth fall, and what reasons did management give?

Trade Desk Blamed The Economy And Itself

Revenue at Trade Desk grew 17.7% from a year earlier in the third quarter of 2025. By the second quarter of 2026, that expansion had slowed to just 3.0%. During the August 6 call, management pointed to two factors behind the miss. Executives said economic conditions had made it harder for some of the world's largest brands to grow, and they acknowledged that Trade Desk had not executed as well as it could have.

Part of the decline occurred in August. The Motley Fool linked the stock's 24% loss that month to the second-quarter report missing estimates and the analyst downgrades that followed. Trade Desk's peers didn't share the slump: Alphabet stock, for one, rose about 50% over the same twelve months.

Where Is Trade Desk Losing Growth?

The current slowdown centers on some of Trade Desk's largest advertisers. For the year to date, advertisers outside the top 500 had grown over 50% year over year, according to management. Executives also pointed to cyclical pressure on two specific groups of advertisers: consumer goods makers and carmakers. These two categories generate around 25% of the company's business. Even so, about half of those advertisers were still growing very well with Trade Desk.

In August, management assumed no meaningful improvement in conditions for the third quarter of 2026, with results for that period still to come. The company guided revenue for that quarter to at least $650 million. This compares to $715 million in the second quarter and about $739 million a year earlier. That guidance implies revenue about 12% lower than in the same quarter of 2025, which would be Trade Desk's first year-over-year quarterly decline in at least three years.

What Has And Has Not Changed At Trade Desk?

Bottom-line profit has slipped. Over the past twelve months, Trade Desk's net margin was 13.6%, down from 15.6% a year before. In August, management guided to less profit for the third quarter. Adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure that leaves out several costs, was guided to about $160 million. The company reported $241 million for this metric in the second quarter.

title: Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: Pfizer vs. UPS

Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: Pfizer vs. UPS
Roxanna Maglangit

UPS
AMZN

Trading disclosure
Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: Pfizer vs. UPS ©halfpoint and Prostock-studio from Canva
Key Takeaways

Pfizer yields 6.3% and UPS yields 7.0%, and both raised their 2026 revenue guidance this summer.

Over the twelve months to June 2026, Pfizer's dividend took 89% of its free cash flow and UPS's took 99%, so neither has much cushion.

UPS raised its dividend per share 0.6% in fiscal 2025, and Pfizer's CEO says its dividend growth returns after the drug patent losses that hit revenue through 2028.

UPS's revenue rose 7.6% in the second quarter of 2026 after it finished cutting Amazon volume. Pfizer's rose 3%, or 1% operationally.

Pfizer (PFE:NYSE) and United Parcel Service (UPS:NYSE) both raised their 2026 revenue guidance this summer. Both also pay the kind of yield income investors go hunting for: 6.3% for Pfizer and 7.0% for UPS.

The catch? Both are handing out nearly every dollar of free cash flow they bring in.

So which is the better high-yield dividend stock?

Pfizer is waiting out its patent losses

Pfizer's newer drugs are carrying the business. Launched and acquired products grew 18% operationally in the second quarter of 2026. COVID-19 sales are shrinking: Pfizer now expects about $4 billion from those products this year, down from about $5 billion in its earlier guidance. Second-quarter revenue was $15.0 billion, up 3% (1% operationally), with adjusted EPS of $0.77 against $0.78 a year before.

The cash behind the dividend has come down hard. Free cash flow went from $29.9 billion in fiscal 2021 to $9.08 billion in fiscal 2025, short of the $9.77 billion Pfizer paid in dividends that year.

Pfizer (PFE): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

Over the twelve months to June 28, 2026, the cash dividend payout ratio was 89%: $9.79 billion of dividends from $10.98 billion of free cash flow. That's thin cover, after 107.7% in fiscal 2025.

Chairman and CEO Albert Bourla says that in "even the most stretched scenarios that we are running, we will be able to maintain our dividend."

Maintain is the word. Pfizer paid $0.86 a share in the first six months of 2026, the same $1.72 annual rate as fiscal 2025. Bourla said growth starts again "after the LOE period," as lost exclusivity on its drugs weighs on revenue through 2028. A bigger hit from those patent losses is the main risk.

UPS has done the hard part

While Pfizer waits out its patent losses, UPS has finished its own reset. In July, it said it had completed its cut of lower-yielding Amazon volume and the network changes that came with it. As CEO Carol Tomé put it on the call, "this reconfiguration was never the destination. It was the foundation."

So far, it's paying off. Second-quarter 2026 revenue was $22.8 billion, up 7.6% from $21.2 billion a year before. Adjusted operating profit rose 12% to $2.1 billion, and UPS raised its full-year outlook.

Since August 28, Realty Income (NYSE:O) has fallen 10.91%. Over the same stretch, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) gained 4.15% and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) rose 5.38%.

Shutterstock

That split sits underneath the S&P 500 target of 8,100 from Scott Chronert, head of US equity strategy at Citi Research. This index target is a forecast about which half of the market stops falling.

Chronert laid out the condition himself: "We need both parts of the market performing. We need that AI influence component that we argue is just over half of the index as well as the other half. That's going to beat to a more traditional macro drummer."

The AI half has already risen, while the other half, priced off the cost of money, has slipped while the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.22%, so the target depends on rate relief as much as on earnings.

AI Stocks and Rate-Sensitive Stocks Are Moving in Opposite Directions

NVIDIA and Microsoft trade on AI capital spending, which lifted NVIDIA's data center revenue 117% last quarter. Banks, REITs, utilities and retailers trade on yields, because higher long rates raise borrowing costs and make dividends less competitive with Treasurys.

Synopsys has ridden a powerful multi year upswing as chip design tools and AI driven workflows move into the spotlight, which puts a sharper focus on whether the current share price lines up with what its cash flows can support. With the stock now around US$494 at the last close, the question is how much of its cash generation story is already baked in.

Over the past 5 years Synopsys has delivered a 59.0% share price gain. As a result, a lot of long term optimism is already reflected and this raises the bar for what its future cash flows need to deliver.

The recent partnership with OpenAI and multi billion dollar deals such as the Amazon agreement may support expectations for stronger and potentially more recurring cash inflows tied to AI centric chip design and silicon IP.

If you'd rather focus on earnings, this one's for you. See why Synopsys's 88.0x P/E tells a different valuation story.

The issue now is whether Synopsys' current market value is adequately backed by the cash flows implied by a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) view over the coming years.

Is Synopsys a Bargain on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here projects what Synopsys might earn for shareholders based on its future cash generation. On the latest figures, the business is producing last twelve month free cash flow of about $2.7b, which signals a sizeable cash engine behind the current US$494.51 share price.

Analyst and model projections point to growing free cash flow into the next decade, with estimated annual cash generation moving further into the multi billion dollar range. The DCF outcome suggests these cash streams support an estimated intrinsic value that is meaningfully above where Synopsys trades today. This implies the market price has not fully caught up with the modeled cash profile. Because the multi year OpenAI partnership and large Amazon agreement both lean on AI heavy chip design and silicon IP, the cash flow upside they point to helps explain why the discounted cash flow view sits ahead of the current quote.
